Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

Ended up early in Narasambhudhi, very overcast with a slight drizzle on and off. Started the birding from near the Nanjangudu-Ch'nagara road (near the road-over-bridge) and walked all the way up to the lake. I was of course welcomed by Rosy Starlings in their 100s along with other Mynas (esp Jungle, Brahminy and CT).     Due to monsoon and likely canal water; the lake is up to its brim, likely reaching its FTL capacity. This is for the first time I did not notice many water / wading birds like Painted Stork, likely moved away due to rising water. As usual the area is mostly deserted and was decent w.r.t to birding activities.      I have also not noticed the regulars like Spot-billed Pelicans, Grey Herons and Egrets. Due to floating vegetation, I did see lots of Eurasian Coots and Jacanas which I had not noticed in large numbers in the past. Overall the recent plantations done illegally on the lake bed was under the water due to sudden filling up of the tank. I did see the fishermen in their huts / shanty, but no fishing activity was evident that morning, but I did notice large number of cat-fishes near the surface.

Was a very bright and sunny morning at Narsambhudhi. Interestingly saw the Rock-eagle Owl nesting near the bund of the canal rock face. The lake is brim, with lots of Black-crowned Night Herons in large numbers. Also observed were extremely large number of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks, but deep inside the partly submerged dead trees at the far south west side of the lake (not accessible via road). Lake was brimming with fish, but did not observe shanty for the fishermen.     Other unfortunate thing, is large tracts of scrub forest on the lake bund have been completely removed. On enquiring the reason; the locals mentioned that it has been removed by the local panchayat for safety of women who transgress this area for work during late/early hours and to prevent cover for potential thugs who have been observed here. It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

#GBBC    GBBC Observation, Yenkathala Grasslands:    Participated in the Great Backyard Bird Count (GBBC) survey at Ramanatha Guntepalli grasslands, locally known as Yenkathala Grasslands, in the late winter period as the season transitions gradually into early spring.    Reached the grasslands around 4:00 PM and birded until sunset (~6:00 PM), covering approximately 8 km by car. Overall bird activity was moderate, but several winter visitors were still present and actively using the habitat. Notable species included Pallid and Montagu’s Harriers in fair numbers, along with Siberian Stonechats and Grey-necked Buntings seen across the grassland patches.    Weather conditions: clear skies, slightly dusty atmosphere. Parts of the grasslands appeared hazy due to recent burning. It was not possible to verify on site whether this was a controlled burn by the Forest Department or due to accidental human-caused fires, though local information suggested it may have been a preventive burn.    The habitat continues to show visible impact from long-standing, unchecked mining activity and expanding human use of the grasslands for other purposes. Compared to earlier years, the overall abundance of birds appears to have reduced noticeably.    These grasslands are also known to support several other species, including Indian (Bengal) Fox, Jungle Cat, and Blackbuck, indicating their ecological importance.  Unless these grasslands receive stronger protection, ideally through formal conservation status, continued habitat degradation may further reduce their value for migratory and resident species. The site remains an important but increasingly threatened wintering ground

Arrived to a chilly morning to the steps area near the temple. It was a hazy and very chilly morning. The crowd of pilgrim was relatively less today. Birded around the temple and little way down the steps. while the temple walk areas are kept very clean, the janitors who clean have no way to dispose safely the waste (plastic and generally pilgrim generated non-bio waste). The only attempt made by them is to dump all the waste along the valley, which has now literally become a garbage dump over the last several years. Its no more sustainable and needs a municipality driven waste disposal or a clean waste management initiative.

Was initially a hazy morning and arrived as the sun was peaking out through the broken clouds. Unfortunately the temple was inundated with people due to some Jaatra (local festivities and gathering) and people dotted all around the temple premises. There was also a blaring megaphone, with music and constant announcement to adher to covid protocols (given the rapid rise in 3rd wave in India due to Omicron), this commotion resulted in extremely low bird activity and I had to restrict my movements to the temple steps alone where I watched for birds standing stationary at times. Likely the birds flew to safer zones. But was still fortunate to spot a flock of Yellow-throated Bulbuls and photographed an individual. All other commonly seen birds like Babblers, Shamas and Thrushes were missing and likely driven out due to the noise. Monday is probably an important calendar day for the temple and I recommended avoiding going on Mondays and public holidays

As usual the area is mostly deserted and was decent w.r.t to birding activities.      I have also not noticed the regulars like Spot-billed Pelicans, Grey Herons and Egrets. Due to floating vegetation, I did see lots of Eurasian Coots and Jacanas which I had not noticed in large numbers in the past. Overall the recent plantations done illegally on the lake bed was under the water due to sudden filling up of the tank. I did see the fishermen in their huts / shanty, but no fishing activity was evident that morning, but I did notice large number of cat-fishes near the surface.

Was a very bright and sunny morning at Narsambhudhi. Interestingly saw the Rock-eagle Owl nesting near the bund of the canal rock face. The lake is brim, with lots of Black-crowned Night Herons in large numbers. Also observed were extremely large number of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks, but deep inside the partly submerged dead trees at the far south west side of the lake (not accessible via road). Lake was brimming with fish, but did not observe shanty for the fishermen.     Other unfortunate thing, is large tracts of scrub forest on the lake bund have been completely removed. On enquiring the reason; the locals mentioned that it has been removed by the local panchayat for safety of women who transgress this area for work during late/early hours and to prevent cover for potential thugs who have been observed here. It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

Ended up early in Narasambhudhi, very overcast with a slight drizzle on and off. Started the birding from near the Nanjangudu-Ch'nagara road (near the road-over-bridge) and walked all the way up to the lake. I was of course welcomed by Rosy Starlings in their 100s along with other Mynas (esp Jungle, Brahminy and CT).     Due to monsoon and likely canal water; the lake is up to its brim, likely reaching its FTL capacity. This is for the first time I did not notice many water / wading birds like Painted Stork, likely moved away due to rising water. As usual the area is mostly deserted and was decent w.r.t to birding activities.      I have also not noticed the regulars like Spot-billed Pelicans, Grey Herons and Egrets. Due to floating vegetation, I did see lots of Eurasian Coots and Jacanas which I had not noticed in large numbers in the past. Overall the recent plantations done illegally on the lake bed was under the water due to sudden filling up of the tank. I did see the fishermen in their huts / shanty, but no fishing activity was evident that morning, but I did notice large number of cat-fishes near the surface.

Was a very bright and sunny morning at Narsambhudhi. Interestingly saw the Rock-eagle Owl nesting near the bund of the canal rock face. The lake is brim, with lots of Black-crowned Night Herons in large numbers. Also observed were extremely large number of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks, but deep inside the partly submerged dead trees at the far south west side of the lake (not accessible via road). Lake was brimming with fish, but did not observe shanty for the fishermen.     Other unfortunate thing, is large tracts of scrub forest on the lake bund have been completely removed. On enquiring the reason; the locals mentioned that it has been removed by the local panchayat for safety of women who transgress this area for work during late/early hours and to prevent cover for potential thugs who have been observed here. It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

Checklist Comments: Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

Was a very bright and sunny morning at Narsambhudhi. Interestingly saw the Rock-eagle Owl nesting near the bund of the canal rock face. Also observed were extremely large number of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks, but deep inside the partly submerged dead trees at the far south west side of the lake (not accessible via road). Lake was brimming with fish, but did not observe shanty for the fishermen.     Other unfortunate thing, is large tracts of scrub forest on the lake bund have been completely removed. On enquiring the reason; the locals mentioned that it has been removed by the local panchayat for safety of women who transgress this area for work during late/early hours and to prevent cover for potential thugs who have been observed here. It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

A truly extraordinary pelagic approach to Narcondam—what first appeared as a distant volcanic silhouette in the far eastern horizon gradually transformed into an emerald island rising steeply out of deep blue waters. The island feels remarkably untouched, with no visible human disturbance apart from a small outpost area.    As we approached the docking zone (~100 ft offshore), Narcondam Hornbills were immediately evident—multiple individuals flying across the canopy and actively foraging. The birds were extensively feeding on fruiting fig trees, with frequent movement between trees suggesting high activity levels in the area. Their presence dominated the soundscape and visual experience around the island.    The habitat is primarily dense tropical rainforest covering much of the island, interspersed with steep rocky faces. Some sections—particularly along exposed slopes—show patches of degraded scrub vegetation. Apart from a few coconut trees likely introduced near the outpost, the vegetation appears largely pristine and undisturbed.    We circumnavigated parts of the island, observing varied terrain including sheer rocky cliffs, forested slopes, and small cave-like formations along the shoreline. The overall impression is of an isolated, ancient ecosystem—intact and functioning with minimal human interference.    Weather during observation: overcast (99–100% cloud cover), temperature ~25°C, light NE breeze, humidity ~63–64%, dew point ~17–18°C.    A rare and humbling experience observing an endemic species in its only natural habitat.

Ended up early in Narasambhudhi, very overcast with a slight drizzle on and off. Started the birding from near the Nanjangudu-Ch'nagara road (near the road-over-bridge) and walked all the way up to the lake. I was of course welcomed by Rosy Starlings in their 100s along with other Mynas (esp Jungle, Brahminy and CT).     Due to monsoon and likely canal water; the lake is up to its brim, likely reaching its FTL capacity. This is for the first time I did not notice many water / wading birds like Painted Stork, likely moved away due to rising water. As usual the area is mostly deserted and was decent w.r.t to birding activities.      I have also not noticed the regulars like Spot-billed Pelicans, Grey Herons and Egrets. Due to floating vegetation, I did see lots of Eurasian Coots and Jacanas which I had not noticed in large numbers in the past. Overall the recent plantations done illegally on the lake bed was under the water due to sudden filling up of the tank. I did see the fishermen in their huts / shanty, but no fishing activity was evident that morning, but I did notice large number of cat-fishes near the surface.

Was a very bright and sunny morning at Narsambhudhi. Interestingly saw the Rock-eagle Owl nesting near the bund of the canal rock face. The lake is brim, with lots of Black-crowned Night Herons in large numbers. Also observed were extremely large number of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks, but deep inside the partly submerged dead trees at the far south west side of the lake (not accessible via road). Lake was brimming with fish, but did not observe shanty for the fishermen.     Other unfortunate thing, is large tracts of scrub forest on the lake bund have been completely removed. On enquiring the reason; the locals mentioned that it has been removed by the local panchayat for safety of women who transgress this area for work during late/early hours and to prevent cover for potential thugs who have been observed here. It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

A truly extraordinary pelagic approach to Narcondam—what first appeared as a distant volcanic silhouette in the far eastern horizon gradually transformed into an emerald island rising steeply out of deep blue waters. The island feels remarkably untouched, with no visible human disturbance apart from a small outpost area.    As we approached the docking zone (~100 ft offshore), Narcondam Hornbills were immediately evident—multiple individuals flying across the canopy and actively foraging. The birds were extensively feeding on fruiting fig trees, with frequent movement between trees suggesting high activity levels in the area. Their presence dominated the soundscape and visual experience around the island.    The habitat is primarily dense tropical rainforest covering much of the island, interspersed with steep rocky faces. Some sections—particularly along exposed slopes—show patches of degraded scrub vegetation. Apart from a few coconut trees likely introduced near the outpost, the vegetation appears largely pristine and undisturbed.    We circumnavigated parts of the island, observing varied terrain including sheer rocky cliffs, forested slopes, and small cave-like formations along the shoreline. The overall impression is of an isolated, ancient ecosystem—intact and functioning with minimal human interference.    Weather during observation: overcast (99–100% cloud cover), temperature ~25°C, light NE breeze, humidity ~63–64%, dew point ~17–18°C.    A rare and humbling experience observing an endemic species in its only natural habitat.

Checklist Comments: Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Location: Musi River Bridge near Narsingi ORR Exit
Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

A truly extraordinary pelagic approach to Narcondam—what first appeared as a distant volcanic silhouette in the far eastern horizon gradually transformed into an emerald island rising steeply out of deep blue waters. The island feels remarkably untouched, with no visible human disturbance apart from a small outpost area.    As we approached the docking zone (~100 ft offshore), Narcondam Hornbills were immediately evident—multiple individuals flying across the canopy and actively foraging. The birds were extensively feeding on fruiting fig trees, with frequent movement between trees suggesting high activity levels in the area. Their presence dominated the soundscape and visual experience around the island.    The habitat is primarily dense tropical rainforest covering much of the island, interspersed with steep rocky faces. Some sections—particularly along exposed slopes—show patches of degraded scrub vegetation. Apart from a few coconut trees likely introduced near the outpost, the vegetation appears largely pristine and undisturbed.    We circumnavigated parts of the island, observing varied terrain including sheer rocky cliffs, forested slopes, and small cave-like formations along the shoreline. The overall impression is of an isolated, ancient ecosystem—intact and functioning with minimal human interference.    Weather during observation: overcast (99–100% cloud cover), temperature ~25°C, light NE breeze, humidity ~63–64%, dew point ~17–18°C.    A rare and humbling experience observing an endemic species in its only natural habitat.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Location: Musi River Bridge near Narsingi ORR Exit
Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

Location: Kadamtala, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, IN (12.392, 92.905)

Checklist Comments: A truly extraordinary pelagic approach to Narcondam—what first appeared as a distant volcanic silhouette in the far eastern horizon gradually transformed into an emerald island rising steeply out of deep blue waters. The island feels remarkably untouched, with no visible human disturbance apart from a small outpost area.    As we approached the docking zone (~100 ft offshore), Narcondam Hornbills were immediately evident—multiple individuals flying across the canopy and actively foraging. The birds were extensively feeding on fruiting fig trees, with frequent movement between trees suggesting high activity levels in the area. Their presence dominated the soundscape and visual experience around the island.    The habitat is primarily dense tropical rainforest covering much of the island, interspersed with steep rocky faces. Some sections—particularly along exposed slopes—show patches of degraded scrub vegetation. Apart from a few coconut trees likely introduced near the outpost, the vegetation appears largely pristine and undisturbed.    We circumnavigated parts of the island, observing varied terrain including sheer rocky cliffs, forested slopes, and small cave-like formations along the shoreline. The overall impression is of an isolated, ancient ecosystem—intact and functioning with minimal human interference.    Weather during observation: overcast (99–100% cloud cover), temperature ~25°C, light NE breeze, humidity ~63–64%, dew point ~17–18°C.    A rare and humbling experience observing an endemic species in its only natural habitat.

Checklist Comments: Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on. #GBBC    GBBC Observation, Yenkathala Grasslands:    Participated in the Great Backyard Bird Count (GBBC) survey at Ramanatha Guntepalli grasslands, locally known as Yenkathala Grasslands, in the late winter period as the season transitions gradually into early spring.    Reached the grasslands around 4:00 PM and birded until sunset (~6:00 PM), covering approximately 8 km by car. Overall bird activity was moderate, but several winter visitors were still present and actively using the habitat. Notable species included Pallid and Montagu’s Harriers in fair numbers, along with Siberian Stonechats and Grey-necked Buntings seen across the grassland patches.    Weather conditions: clear skies, slightly dusty atmosphere. Parts of the grasslands appeared hazy due to recent burning. It was not possible to verify on site whether this was a controlled burn by the Forest Department or due to accidental human-caused fires, though local information suggested it may have been a preventive burn.    The habitat continues to show visible impact from long-standing, unchecked mining activity and expanding human use of the grasslands for other purposes. Compared to earlier years, the overall abundance of birds appears to have reduced noticeably.    These grasslands are also known to support several other species, including Indian (Bengal) Fox, Jungle Cat, and Blackbuck, indicating their ecological importance.  Unless these grasslands receive stronger protection, ideally through formal conservation status, continued habitat degradation may further reduce their value for migratory and resident species. The site remains an important but increasingly threatened wintering ground

Ended up early in Narasambhudhi, very overcast with a slight drizzle on and off. Started the birding from near the Nanjangudu-Ch'nagara road (near the road-over-bridge) and walked all the way up to the lake. I was of course welcomed by Rosy Starlings in their 100s along with other Mynas (esp Jungle, Brahminy and CT).     Due to monsoon and likely canal water; the lake is up to its brim, likely reaching its FTL capacity. This is for the first time I did not notice many water / wading birds like Painted Stork, likely moved away due to rising water. As usual the area is mostly deserted and was decent w.r.t to birding activities.      I have also not noticed the regulars like Spot-billed Pelicans, Grey Herons and Egrets. Due to floating vegetation, I did see lots of Eurasian Coots and Jacanas which I had not noticed in large numbers in the past. Overall the recent plantations done illegally on the lake bed was under the water due to sudden filling up of the tank. I did see the fishermen in their huts / shanty, but no fishing activity was evident that morning, but I did notice large number of cat-fishes near the surface.

Was a very bright and sunny morning at Narsambhudhi. Interestingly saw the Rock-eagle Owl nesting near the bund of the canal rock face. The lake is brim, with lots of Black-crowned Night Herons in large numbers. Also observed were extremely large number of Spot-billed Pelicans and Painted Storks, but deep inside the partly submerged dead trees at the far south west side of the lake (not accessible via road). Lake was brimming with fish, but did not observe shanty for the fishermen.     Other unfortunate thing, is large tracts of scrub forest on the lake bund have been completely removed. On enquiring the reason; the locals mentioned that it has been removed by the local panchayat for safety of women who transgress this area for work during late/early hours and to prevent cover for potential thugs who have been observed here. It is likely going to have a severe impact on the bird life and migration in winters.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

Checklist Comments: A truly extraordinary pelagic approach to Narcondam—what first appeared as a distant volcanic silhouette in the far eastern horizon gradually transformed into an emerald island rising steeply out of deep blue waters. The island feels remarkably untouched, with no visible human disturbance apart from a small outpost area.    As we approached the docking zone (~100 ft offshore), Narcondam Hornbills were immediately evident—multiple individuals flying across the canopy and actively foraging. The birds were extensively feeding on fruiting fig trees, with frequent movement between trees suggesting high activity levels in the area. Their presence dominated the soundscape and visual experience around the island.    The habitat is primarily dense tropical rainforest covering much of the island, interspersed with steep rocky faces. Some sections—particularly along exposed slopes—show patches of degraded scrub vegetation. Apart from a few coconut trees likely introduced near the outpost, the vegetation appears largely pristine and undisturbed.    We circumnavigated parts of the island, observing varied terrain including sheer rocky cliffs, forested slopes, and small cave-like formations along the shoreline. The overall impression is of an isolated, ancient ecosystem—intact and functioning with minimal human interference.    Weather during observation: overcast (99–100% cloud cover), temperature ~25°C, light NE breeze, humidity ~63–64%, dew point ~17–18°C.    A rare and humbling experience observing an endemic species in its only natural habitat.

Visited Kokapet Lake for ~90 minutes as part of the AWC 2026 effort with a group of 8. On the surface, this lake looks like it’s “improving”: the walkway is well-built, landscaping is pleasant, and the space has clearly been shaped into a family-friendly public area. There also appears to be real intent from NGOs/private players to revive the lake compared to what it was a couple of years ago.    But we shouldn’t confuse a nicer promenade with ecological recovery. The lake still appears heavily impacted by sewage inflow, and waterbird use remains lower than expected, especially for a lake of this size. Some interventions—tree planting at the edges, fountains, and creating islands—may be well-meaning, but without a clear, scientific habitat + water-quality plan, they risk becoming cosmetic “lake makeovers.”    Kokapet is a strong candidate for doing things right: sewage interception, water-quality remediation, invasive control, habitat zoning, shoreline buffers, and enforcement to prevent trespass and re-pollution.    The intent is good. The next step has to be science + governance, not just aesthetics.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

Visited Narasingi Nalla Cheruvu during the AWC 2026 period with 8 birders. The lake has the bones of a scenic wetland, but right now it reads like a case study in urban neglect. The water appeared fluorescent green in sections, strongly suggesting heavy algal load/eutrophication tied to high nutrient pollution. At points near the outlet, the green discharge looked especially intense, and the overall water quality felt visibly stressed.    Unsurprisingly, waterbird use was very limited. Apart from a few species (e.g., Little Grebes) and some shorebirds around the margins, the lake felt biologically subdued—exactly what you’d expect when habitat quality and oxygen levels are compromised.    The lake is also being ringed by a massive construction footprint, turning the wetland into an isolated “pocket” surrounded by a concrete jungle. That fragmentation, plus disturbance, accelerates deterioration.    This site needs more than beautification. It needs pollution source control, inlet/outlet monitoring, trash removal, invasive management, buffer protection, and local stewardship—before it becomes just a green-tinted sump with a view.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

#GBBC    GBBC Observation, Yenkathala Grasslands:    Participated in the Great Backyard Bird Count (GBBC) survey at Ramanatha Guntepalli grasslands, locally known as Yenkathala Grasslands, in the late winter period as the season transitions gradually into early spring.    Reached the grasslands around 4:00 PM and birded until sunset (~6:00 PM), covering approximately 8 km by car. Overall bird activity was moderate, but several winter visitors were still present and actively using the habitat. Notable species included Pallid and Montagu’s Harriers in fair numbers, along with Siberian Stonechats and Grey-necked Buntings seen across the grassland patches.    Weather conditions: clear skies, slightly dusty atmosphere. Parts of the grasslands appeared hazy due to recent burning. It was not possible to verify on site whether this was a controlled burn by the Forest Department or due to accidental human-caused fires, though local information suggested it may have been a preventive burn.    The habitat continues to show visible impact from long-standing, unchecked mining activity and expanding human use of the grasslands for other purposes. Compared to earlier years, the overall abundance of birds appears to have reduced noticeably.    These grasslands are also known to support several other species, including Indian (Bengal) Fox, Jungle Cat, and Blackbuck, indicating their ecological importance.  Unless these grasslands receive stronger protection, ideally through formal conservation status, continued habitat degradation may further reduce their value for migratory and resident species. The site remains an important but increasingly threatened wintering ground

A truly extraordinary pelagic approach to Narcondam—what first appeared as a distant volcanic silhouette in the far eastern horizon gradually transformed into an emerald island rising steeply out of deep blue waters. The island feels remarkably untouched, with no visible human disturbance apart from a small outpost area.    As we approached the docking zone (~100 ft offshore), Narcondam Hornbills were immediately evident—multiple individuals flying across the canopy and actively foraging. The birds were extensively feeding on fruiting fig trees, with frequent movement between trees suggesting high activity levels in the area. Their presence dominated the soundscape and visual experience around the island.    The habitat is primarily dense tropical rainforest covering much of the island, interspersed with steep rocky faces. Some sections—particularly along exposed slopes—show patches of degraded scrub vegetation. Apart from a few coconut trees likely introduced near the outpost, the vegetation appears largely pristine and undisturbed.    We circumnavigated parts of the island, observing varied terrain including sheer rocky cliffs, forested slopes, and small cave-like formations along the shoreline. The overall impression is of an isolated, ancient ecosystem—intact and functioning with minimal human interference.    Weather during observation: overcast (99–100% cloud cover), temperature ~25°C, light NE breeze, humidity ~63–64%, dew point ~17–18°C.    A rare and humbling experience observing an endemic species in its only natural habitat.

Checklist Comments: Visited this stretch as part of the Asian Waterbird Census (AWC) 2026 window (20 Dec 2025–6 Feb 2026) with a group of 8 birders. Morning was chilly (~14°C) with cloud cover, scattered clouds, and light haze. Winter visitors are present along the edges and shallows, and it’s always encouraging to see birds holding on.    But the larger picture is grim. The Musi here increasingly resembles a sewage channel, with obvious untreated inflow and degraded water quality. What’s most alarming is the intensity of construction on both banks—habitat is being squeezed from every direction: disturbance, noise, loss of natural shoreline, and the slow “hardening” of edges that waterbirds rely on.    Over the years, this area has clearly seen a decline in both numbers and diversity, and the reasons are visible: pollution, land pressure/encroachment, and rapid urbanization at a pace Hyderabad hasn’t seen before.    If we want sustainability to be part of the city’s success story, the Musi needs sewage interception, bank buffers, enforcement, and genuine ecological restoration, not more concrete.

The morning at Yenkathala grasslands was brisk and chilly, with a thick cloud cover and a soft haze lingering from the night’s downpour. The rains had drenched the landscape, leaving the grasslands a vibrant shade of green. As usual, the local sheep herders had set up temporary barricades to graze their large flocks—likely migrants from distant areas seeking fresh pasture.    Today brought some truly exciting sightings. I was fortunate to spot an Indian (Bengal) Fox and, for the very first time here, a small group of Blackbucks—three in total, including a striking male and two females. These moments made the chill and early start more than worthwhile.    Yet, amidst the beauty, a note of concern: the grasslands are rapidly changing. Patches are being cleared and converted for agricultural use, and it’s unclear whether these developments are regulated or happening unchecked. The time feels ripe for conservation measures—without protection, we risk losing these remarkable habitats and the wildlife they sustain.

Ended up early in Narasambhudhi, very overcast with a slight drizzle on and off. Started the birding from near the Nanjangudu-Ch'nagara road (near the road-over-bridge) and walked all the way up to the lake. I was of course welcomed by Rosy Starlings in their 100s along with other Mynas (esp Jungle, Brahminy and CT).     Due to monsoon and likely canal water; the lake is up to its brim, likely reaching its FTL capacity. This is for the first time I did not notice many water / wading birds like Painted Stork, likely moved away due to rising water. As usual the area is mostly deserted and was decent w.r.t to birding activities.      I have also not noticed the regulars like Spot-billed Pelicans, Grey Herons and Egrets. Due to floating vegetation, I did see lots of Eurasian Coots and Jacanas which I had not noticed in large numbers in the past. Overall the recent plantations done illegally on the lake bed was under the water due to sudden filling up of the tank. I did see the fishermen in their huts / shanty, but no fishing activity was evident that morning, but I did notice large number of cat-fishes near the surface.
